newsitem.title: GREECE: AUDIT OF ATHENS BROKERS RAISES CONFIDENTIALITY.
newsitem.headline: AUDIT OF ATHENS BROKERS RAISES CONFIDENTIALITY.

text.p: Athens stock brokerages are under a 48-hour deadline to provide information on client shares in their custody, raising some concern on client confidentiality.

Three international auditing companies -- Ernst & Young, Deloitte and Touche and Peat Marwick -- will begin auditing the exchange's 65 members on Friday following the Delta Securities settlement scandal.

Delta's attempt to settle at the bourse clearing house with 2.6 billion drachmas in bad cheques triggered a crisis which rocked the stock exchange to its foundations and stopped almost all trading for four days earlier this month.
The capital markets commission has ordered the brokers to furnish the auditors with details of all client shares in their custody and state where the shares are currently kept.
But brokers have raised the issue of client confidentiality and have given mixed responses as to how they will proceed.

The Association of Athens Stock Exchange Members (SMEHA) must also supply auditors with detailed information on their own trading account specifying all securities -- stocks and bonds -- presently owned.

The capital markets commission, the market watchdog, has said the detailed trading activity of all clients, including those with zero balances as of October 1, must be provided when the auditors begin to check records at brokers offices.
SMEHA has said it has no problem with confidentiality as long as the audits are conducted in situ and no client records leave the offices.

"The audits will take place at brokers offices. As long as the auditing firms commit to the good use of confidential information -- client names and trading history -- and since this is an order by the authorities, SMEHA has no problem on confidentiality grounds," SMEHA president Panagiotis Kondalexis told Reuters.
But not all SMEHA brokers were as keen to embrace an open book policy.
"There is an issue of confidentiality. Many brokers have agreed to provide account code numbers and not names at first stage," said Nick Iatrou at Hellenic Securities.

"On the other hand, we cannot deny providing client names behind the accounts. Simply, a lot of brokers will not provide them immediately until it is specifically requested by the auditors. Clients deserve confidentiality," he said.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis announced the plans for a full audit of all brokerages in parliament last week while the Delta scandal was raging.
"Since this has to be done, the auditors are responsible for respecting confidentiality," Kondalexis said.
The national economy ministry ordered a separate audit, by its own officials, of 10 brokerages after the Delta Scandal had shut the bourse for four days.
Many SMEHA brokers had said that the Delta scandal was part of a wider campaign of organised short-selling and price manipulation by some clients, brokers or brokerages.

SMEHA stopped all trading at the bourse to back its demand that seemingly reluctant bourse and government authorities take charge of their responsibilities to audit brokers and tighten regulation of the clearing house.
Investigating magistrate Costas Ganiatsos, who is overseeing the probe into the Delta scandal, confiscated securities found at the company's offices on Tuesday. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
